title: the things they remember
author: Sharp, Colby
summary: This short reflective piece uses the return of a former student — now training to become a teacher herself — to demonstrate the lasting power of the classroom read-aloud tradition. When the former student presses the author about what else he's reading to his current class, she eventually names a book, The Line Tender, that had such an emotional impact on her years earlier that she wrote to the author, received a reply, and hosted an author visit — a memory she still cherishes years later. The author uses this to make a direct claim about the value of a practice he sees eroding: read-alouds are 'one of the most powerful traditions we have in our schools,' yet are happening less often, with some teachers criticized for taking class time for them. The piece closes as a direct thank-you and encouragement to teachers who continue the practice, framing it as building community and irreplaceable memory rather than merely covering curriculum content.
points: A former student, now training to be a teacher herself, spontaneously recalls a specific book (The Line Tender) read aloud years earlier as the one that had the most lasting impact on her.
That single read-aloud experience led the student to write to the book's author, receive a reply, and eventually host an author visit to the classroom — a memory she says she still cherishes.
The piece names read-alouds as 'one of the most powerful traditions we have in our schools,' explicitly framing them as more than entertainment or filler time.
A direct concern is raised that read-alouds are happening less and less, with some teachers criticized for spending class time on them.

The closing argument reframes the value of read-alouds as community- and memory-building — students remember specific stories and the shared experience of hearing them years after the fact, in a way other instructional formats may not replicate.
quotes: She asked me what I was reading aloud to the classroom. I told her that we were starting with Jasmine Warga's A Rover's Story. She followed up with the question, what else? And what else. And what else.
Finally, she said, "Why aren't you reading them The Line Tender?" I smiled. I had forgotten what an impact that read aloud had on her and her classmates when I read them the book aloud.
She told my class about how the author ended up visiting our classroom, and that she still cherishes her signed copy of the book.

The read aloud is one of the most powerful traditions we have in our schools. For some wild and sad reason, it is happening less and less, and in some schools teachers are given a bunch of crap for wanting to take time out of their day to read aloud to kids.
Thank you for reading aloud. Kids will never forget those stories, those memories, and the community created through the stories we share together.
